title: Salman Khan Wants a Turquoise Bracelet Banned From the Movies. The Delhi High Court Just Told Him to Wait.
excerpt: A low-budget film called 'Kala Hiran' has India's biggest star in court, the director firing back with 'Salman isn't God', and a producer claiming death threats from a Pakistani terrorist. The hearing now stretches to July 1.
body:
It started with a bracelet.

A turquoise stone, set in silver, the kind **Salman Khan** has worn on screen and off for two decades until it became as much a part of his iconography as the bare torso and the bird whistle. When the first-look posters of a film called ***Kala Hiran: The Battle for Legacy*** surfaced online, fans did the math in seconds. A brooding hero. A blackbuck. A signature bracelet. A story that hums, unmistakably, in the key of Salman's 1998 poaching case. The internet decided this was a Salman film without Salman in it — and Salman, it turns out, agrees, which is precisely the problem.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=ZTIG5sJiOZc</youtube>



> **"Salman's senior advocate **Sandeep Sethi** argued the obvious heavyweight position — *"He is producing a film on my life."**



On Friday, June 19, the **Delhi High Court** declined to hand the superstar the one thing he wanted most: an emergency order to stop the film cold. Justice Madhu Jain heard both sides, noted that the producers had received the application only two days earlier, and pushed the whole matter to July 1. Salman's senior advocate **Sandeep Sethi** argued the obvious heavyweight position — *"He is producing a film on my life. He has no right. I have not authorised him."* The court's response was, in effect: take a number.

> "Salman Khan isn't God, he can't stop me." — Bharat S Shrinate, director of Kala Hiran

That line, delivered by director **Bharat S Shrinate** to News18, is the reason this story has legs. Most filmmakers facing a legal notice from the most powerful man in Hindi cinema would issue a sheepish clarification and quietly recolor the posters. Shrinate did the opposite. On the bracelet — the literal centerpiece of Salman's complaint — he was almost gleeful: *"The bracelet isn't a patented accessory. If Salman feels only he can wear it, he should get it patented. It shouldn't be available anywhere else in the world."* He insists the character isn't Salman, the film isn't a biopic, and the resemblance is in the eye of a beholder who wants to see it. *"This is just a film,"* he says, which is the kind of thing people say when a film is very much not just a film.

Salman's team sees personality rights, reputational damage, and a project trying to monetize his face without paying for it. The petition flags the turquoise bracelet, the gun-toting visuals, and the danger of prejudicing a poaching case still pending before the Rajasthan High Court. It's a real legal argument, dressed in real stakes — the kind of personality-rights fight that **Amitabh Bachchan**, **Anil Kapoor** and, just this week, **Preity Zinta** have all taken to court as India wakes up to how loosely a star's likeness can be borrowed.

And then the plot, already operatic, tipped fully into masala. Producer **Amit Jani** — who once tore up a Salman legal notice on camera — claims he's now receiving death threats, including one he attributes to a declared Pakistani terrorist, Shahzad Bhatti, allegedly threatening a drone-and-grenade attack while "taking Salman Khan's side." Jani says he's logged a second threat within twenty-four hours and alerted the Home Ministry, the Rajasthan Police and the CRPF. Whether you read this as a genuine security scare or the most aggressive marketing campaign a low-budget film has ever mounted, it is doing what no poster could: keeping ***Kala Hiran*** in every headline.

For the diaspora watching from New Jersey to Southall, the spectacle is irresistible precisely because it's about the spectacle of stardom itself. Can a megastar own the visual grammar of his own scandals? Does a bracelet belong to a man or to the public domain the moment a million fans associate it with him? These are the questions that usually get argued in a film studies seminar, and here they are being argued in Court No. whatever, with a smuggler subplot.

The film, undeterred, is barreling toward release. The teaser is out. The producers are refusing temporary relief. And the man at the center of it all, who has spent thirty years being the immovable object of Bollywood, has just been told by a judge that even immovable objects wait their turn.

July 1 is the date to circle. Either the court hands Salman his injunction and ***Kala Hiran*** becomes the most famous film no one got to see, or it doesn't, and a small movie about a big star walks into theatres carrying the priceless gift of his fury. Either way, somewhere out there, a turquoise bracelet is having the best week of its life.
